Usually, these infections are caused by breathing infectious particles into the lungs (respiratory tract). SIGNS AND SYMPTOMS   Symptoms depend on the age of the child and the cause of the pneumonia. Common symptoms are:  · Cough.  · Fever.  · Chills.  · Chest pain.  · Abdominal pain.  · Feeling worn out when doing usual activities (fatigue).  · Loss of hunger (appetite).  · Lack of interest in play.  · Fast, shallow breathing.  · Shortness of breath.  A cough may continue for several weeks even after the child feels better. This is the normal way the body clears out the infection.  DIAGNOSIS   Pneumonia may be diagnosed by a physical exam. A chest X-ray examination may be done. Other tests of your child's blood, urine, or sputum may be done to find the specific cause of the pneumonia.  TREATMENT   Pneumonia that is caused by bacteria is treated with antibiotic medicine. Antibiotics do not treat viral infections. Most cases of pneumonia can be treated at home with medicine and rest. More severe cases need hospital treatment.  HOME CARE INSTRUCTIONS   · Cough suppressants may be used as directed by your child's health care provider. Presented as a trauma with splenic laceration. Exploratory laparotomy was recommended. He was intubated in the trauma bay and received 2 units PRBC with 2 L IVF prior to transfer to CT scan. BP remained stable in CT where he was noted to have a grade V splenic laceration and a left sided pneumothorax. He was emergently transferred to the OR for Laparotomy    PROCEDURE:  The patient was escorted to the operating room by anesthesia and placed supine on the OR table. Pre-op abx were give, SCDs were placed and he underwent induction of general anesthesia. He had previously been intubated in the trauma bay and nunez and OGT had already been inserted. A timeout was called to identify the correct patient and procedure.   The abdomen was prepped and draped in sterile fashion. An upper midline laparotomy incision was made with the 10 blade scalpel and carried down to the fascia sharply. The fascia was scored with the cautery, lifted with vitaly clamps and the peritoneum was sharply entered. The remainder of the fascia was opened with cautery.  Once the abomen was entered there was a large volume hemoperitoneum that was suctioned. The left upper quadrant was packed with laparotomy pads and clot was removed. A Cruz retractor was inserted and the abdominal wall retracted to visualize the spleen which appeared shattered 
andlateral attachments had already been autodissected by hematoma. Clots were evacuated and the spleen was medialized by bluntly taking down any remaining attachments to the colon and lateral abdominal wall. Most of the gastrosplenic ligament was already avulsed from the spleen. The hilum was identified and a Malian clamp was placed across. The hilum was transected with curved solitario scissors. The spleen was removed and sent to pathology. All vascular pedicles were ligated with 0-silk suture. Bleeding points were cauterized. Packs were replaced in the left upper quadrant and slowly removed to identify any further bleeding. In order to identify the splenic vessels more carefully, the gastrocolic ligament was opened with the Enseal device and the lesser sac was entered. There was some clot coming from the lesser sac. The pancreas was identified posterior to the stomach and appeared intact with mild contusion. The splenic vessels were unable to be safely identified here due to the patients body habitus and large amount of visceral adipose. We were then able to trace back the splenic vessels from the cut hilum, dissect around them and place an 0-silk suture ligature.. The abdomen was copiously irrigated to remove all remaining old blood and clots. All four quadrants were inspected for any further signs of bleeding. There was still a large volume of hemoperitoneum in the right upper quadrant that was evacuated. The liver was palpated, no injury was identified. The gallbladder and hepatic flexure and colon mesentery appeared intact. The right and left lower quadrants as well ans the pelvis were also inspected. Remaining blood and clots were evacuated and no continued bleeding was noted. There did not appear to be any other injuries. We irrigated the abdomen once more. Once satisfied with hemostasis, the midline fascia of the incision was closed with running 0-looped PDS x2. The wound was irrigated and skin was closed with 
margy and covered with sterile dressings.     A left sided chest tube was then inserted. An incision was made at the 4th intercostal space at the anterior axillary line with a 10 blade.subcutaneous tissues were dissected with a tonsil and the pleural cavity was bluntly entered. The lung was palpated and swept away form the thoracic cavity. A 32 Fr chest tube was inserted and secured with an 0-silk suture. The chest tube was connected to an atrium and placed on suction. Sterile dressings were applied. The patient tolerated the procedure well and was sent to SICU in critical condition, Butler Memorial Hospitalng intubated. Sponge counts were not able to be made correctly, thus an intra-operative xray was performed which did not identify any retained foreign body. Peripherally Inserted Central Catheters and Midline Catheters   WHAT YOU NEED TO KNOW:   A catheter is a small tube used to give treatments and to take blood. The catheter is guided into place through a peripheral vein in your upper arm. Peripheral veins lead from your arms and legs to your heart. A peripherally inserted central catheter (PICC) is guided into a vein near the heart. A midline catheter is guided into a vein below the armpit.   DISCHARGE INSTRUCTIONS:   Prevent catheter-associated infections:  The area around your catheter may get infected, or you may get an infection in your bloodstream. A catheter-associated infection is caused by bacteria (germs) getting into your bloodstream through your catheter. Infections from catheters can lead to severe illness. The following are ways you can help prevent an infection:  � Wash your hands:  Use soap or an alcohol-based hand rub to clean your hands. Clean your hands before and after you touch the catheter or the catheter site. Ask your healthcare provider for information on how to wash your hands. Remind anyone who cares for your catheter to wash their hands.     � Wear medical gloves:  Wear clean medical gloves when you touch your catheter or change bandages.     � Limit contact:  Do not touch or handle your catheter unless you need to care for it. Do not pull, push on, or move the catheter when you clean your skin or change the bandage.    � Clean your skin:  Clean the skin around your catheter every day and just before you change your bandage. Ask your healthcare provider what to use when you clean your skin.     � Check for infection:  Check your skin every day for signs of infection, such as pain, redness, swelling, and oozing. Contact your healthcare provider if you see these signs.    � Cover the area:  Keep a sterile bandage over the catheter site. Change the bandage as directed or when it is loose, wet, dirty, or falls off. Change your bandage in a 
place away from open windows, heating ducts, and fans. Be sure it is well-lit, clean, and free of dust. Clean the skin under the bandage with the solution your healthcare provider suggests. Let the area dry before you put on the new bandage.    � Keep the area dry:  Do not let your catheter or catheter site get wet. Wrap your arm with plastic and seal with medical tape before you bathe. Ask if you should take showers instead of baths.  Care for your PICC or midline catheter:  Your healthcare provider may want you to do the following to reduce your risk of infection or complications:  � Clean your catheter parts:  Clean the caps, hubs, and injection ports before you attach and after you remove tubing from your catheter. Open the package that contains the new alcohol pad. Put on new medical gloves. Use a new alcohol pad for each part you clean. Throw away used alcohol pads.    � Flush your catheter:  Your healthcare provider may give you syringes filled with saline (salt water) or heparin to flush your catheter. Heparin is a medicine that helps prevent blood clots from forming inside the catheter. Heparin can cause an allergic reaction and bleeding problems.     � Attach the syringe that contains the flushing solution to the end of the catheter tubing. Slowly push the fluid out of the syringe and into the catheter. Throw away the syringe. Clean the end of the catheter or cap with a new alcohol pad.    � Do not force the fluid. Force could damage the catheter, or release a blood clot from the end of the catheter. Straighten any kinks in the tubing. Contact your healthcare provider if it is still hard to push fluid into the catheter.    � Change the caps and medicine tubing:  You may need to use extra tubing to get medicine. Ask your healthcare provider how often to change the caps and the medicine tubing.     � Clamp the catheter:  You may need to clamp your catheter at certain times, such as when the tubing is being 
changed. The catheter is clamped to help prevent air from getting in.    � Loop extra tubing:  Loosely loop the tubing together. Secure it to your arm with medical tape. This will help prevent the PICC or midline catheter from being pulled out by accident.  Follow up with your healthcare provider as directed:  Write down your questions so you remember to ask them during your visits.   NSAIDs:  This medicine will help decrease pain and redness where the catheter enters your skin. You can buy NSAIDs without a prescription. NSAIDs can cause stomach bleeding or kidney problems if you do not take them correctly. Always read the medicine label and follow the directions before you use this medicine.  Warm compresses:  The area where the catheter was inserted may feel sore. A warm compress can help to decrease pain and swelling in your arm. Wet a small towel with warm water. Wring out the extra water. Wrap the cloth in plastic, and put it on the area. Use the compress 4 times a day, for 10 minutes each time. Prop your arm up on pillows when you are sitting or lying down. This will decrease swelling.   Contact your healthcare provider if:   � You have a fever.     � The catheter site is red, warm, painful, or oozing fluid.    � You see blood on your bandage and the amount is increasing.     � The veins in your neck or chest bulge.     � You cannot flush your catheter, or you feel pain when you flush your catheter.     � You see that the catheter is getting shorter or it falls out. Put pressure over the site with a clean towel before you contact your healthcare provider.    � You see a hole or a crack in your catheter. Clamp your catheter above the damage before you contact your healthcare provider.     � You have questions about how to care for your catheter.    � You run out of supplies to care for your skin or catheter.  Return to the emergency department if:   � You feel pain in your arm, neck, shoulder, or 
chest.    � The catheter site turns cold, changes color, or you cannot feel it.    � You cough up blood.    � You see blisters on the skin near the catheter site.  � 2017 Popdust. SURGEON:  Min Newell MD    ANESTHESIA:  General.    ESTIMATED BLOOD LOSS:  400 mL.    COMPLICATIONS ENCOUNTERED:  None.    SPECIMEN SENT:  Wall of aneurysm, was sent for tissue culture.    INDICATIONS:  A 39-year-old male patient who presented to the emerRiver Valley Medical Center  department with hemorrhage from a laceration in the right antecubital  fossa which was arterial, brisk and required application of two  tourniquets by prehospital care providers.    DESCRIPTION OF PROCEDURE:  The patient was brought to the operating  room, placed in the supine position.  General anesthesia was induced.   He was prepped and draped in a standard fashion.  Preoperative time-out  was conducted.    Attention was turned onto the right upper extremity.  The two  tourniquets placed by prehospital care were removed and a pneumatic  tourniquet was placed and inflated to 250 mmHg.  Next, the brachial  artery proximal to the injury was exposed through a standard  longitudinal incision and it was dissected circumferentially and vessel  loop proximally and distally.  It was occluded with a vascular clamp 
and  pneumatic tourniquet was then released.  Attention was then turned to  the area distal to the injury where the brachial artery distal to the  aneurysm was exposed through a longitudinal incision, dissected  circumferentially.  This incision was then extended proximally to the  area of the pseudoaneurysm with proximal and distal control obtained.   The pseudoaneurysm was debrided identifying and ligating multiple  arterial and venous branches.  Once hemostasis was obtained, a length of  saphenous vein was harvested and preserved and on-table angiogram was  performed through the distal brachial artery to verify the vessel and  assessed the runoff, dominant runoff appeared to be through the ulnar  artery to the hand but the distal radial artery and pedal arch did not  opacify.  A brachial artery to brachial artery bypass was then performed  with the greater saphenous vein tunneling the saphenous vein medially  outside the area of obvious infection.  The proximal anastomosis was  sewn end-to-side with continuous 6-0 running suture.  The vein was then  flushed and it was sewn end-to-side to the distal anastomosis.  The  bypass graft was opened and good arterial flow was assessed including  strong Doppler signal at the ulnar artery, and the wrist and the hand  became warm and with good capillary refill.  The wounds were irrigated  with antibiotic saline solution and closed primarily with heavy 2-0  nylon suture. DISCHARGE DIAGNOSES:  

1. Diverticulitis, refractory to medical treatment, diverticular abscess, not

amenable to percutaneous drainage due to small size and location behind the bladder

and surrounded by bowel. 

2. Postoperative bleeding requiring repeat laparoscopy without definitive finding of

bleeding site, although suspicious areas cauterized, hemostatic agents Allan

applied. 



HISTORY AND HOSPITAL COURSE:  A 50-year-old male patient admitted for abdominal

pain.  He has been treated for diverticulitis by Dr. Dilip Castanon with several

rounds of antibiotics since March.  He was referred to Dr. Fransisco Bergman for

urinary symptoms because he had pain on urination.  He was treated for 2 rounds of

antibiotics for prostatitis.  He continued to have pain, presented to the emergency

room, found to have a small 2.5 x 3 cm abscess behind the bladder surrounded by

bowel, not amenable due to a small size and location for percutaneous drainage.  The

patient was treated with intravenous antibiotics.  By the first 24 hours, he felt

better.  He then felt worse.  Decision was made for laparoscopic evaluation, which

he underwent on 10/03/2019 at about noon.  He had a small abscess, it was drained.

The sigmoid colon was plastered to the bladder and pelvic wall.  Attempted to take

this down, but it was too tightly adherent and it was felt that as the patient did

not want definitive colon resection at this time, it was hoped that drainage of his

abscess would relieve his symptoms and avoid a colon resection at this time.

Postoperatively, the patient initially did well in the recovery room with normal

blood pressure.  Initially, did well on transfer to the floor with normal blood

pressure.  He then began having acutely hypotensive later in the evening.  His

hemoglobin had dropped from 14 to 11.7 preoperatively and 9.7 postoperatively, and

because he was hypotensive and pale, he was taken to the operating room, where

laparoscopy revealed intra-abdominal blood that was evacuated.  He was given 1 unit

of blood normalizing his blood pressure.  The definitive bleeding site was not

found, although there were few areas that appeared possibly be suspicious and they

were cauterized.  Hemostatic agents were placed in the areas of initial dissection.

A drain was left in place.  Postoperatively, he did well.  His hemoglobin stabilized

and he was discharged home with a hemoglobin of 8.7.  He was sent home with

Augmentin for 10 days.  He is to follow up in my office in 1 week.  By the time of

discharge, he was feeling much better.  The preoperative pain resolved.  The patient

had a colonoscopy in the past with Dr. Mayorga five years ago, and at that time it was

told he had diverticulosis and a few polyps.  At this point, roze will see me in 1

week.  Continue oral antibiotics, and we will discuss the need for any future

surgical intervention based on his clinical course.

EVENT DATE: 2018

SURGEON: Chun Hicks MD

ANESTHESIOLOGIST: Santi Andres MD

ANESTHESIA: General endotracheal.

census enumerator: IGNACIO Zimmerman





PREOPERATIVE DIAGNOSIS  

L4-L5 degenerative disk disease with spondylolisthesis and neurogenic 
claudication.  



POSTOPERATIVE DIAGNOSIS 

L4-L5 degenerative disk disease with spondylolisthesis and neurogenic 
claudication.  



PROCEDURE PERFORMED 

L4-L5 laminectomy and L4-L5 posterolateral instrumented fusion.  



IV FLUIDS 

1700 mL. 



ESTIMATED BLOOD LOSS 

150 mL.



IMPLANTS

6.5 mm x 45 mm Reline pedicle screws from NuVasive x 4, a 35 mm connecting priyanka 
and a 40 mm connecting priyanka also from NuVasive and locking caps x 4 from 
NuVasive.  



SPECIMENS

None.



DRAINS

None.



COMPLICATIONS

An incidental durotomy occurred, and will be described later in the procedure.  



INDICATIONS FOR SURGERY

Mr. Griffin an 80-year-old avid cyclist who presented to my clinic with complaint 
of worsening right greater than left pain, numbness and tingling in an L5 
distribution down bilateral lower extremities.  In addition to this, he noted 
decreased walking tolerance secondary to heaviness and tiredness in his legs.  
His physical examination was essentially unremarkable, but his MRI showed 
severe spinal stenosis at the L4-L5 level, and flexion and extension x-rays 
showed significantly dynamic spondylolisthesis at L4-L5.  Mr. Griffin had failed 
physical therapy, medications and activity modifications, and was therefore 
offered and elected to undergo L4-L5 laminectomy and fusion. 



Prior to surgery, I explained in detail to the patient the possible risks of 
surgery.  This includes the risk of bleeding, infection, damage to surrounding 
structures, persistent and/or worsening pain, nerve root injury, spinal fluid 
leak, meningitis, , blindness, sexual dysfunction, autonomic nervous 
system dysfunction as well as other unforeseen medical and surgical 
complications. An understanding that spinal surgery is more predictive in 
improving extremity discomfort than axial spine pain was stressed.  



DESCRIPTION OF PROCEDURE   

On the date of surgery, the patient was admitted to the preoperative hold area, 
and all questions were answered.  The operative site was identified and marked 
by myself.  The patient was brought in good condition to the operating room, 
and after succumbing to anesthesia, was placed in the prone position on a 
Grady table.  All bony protuberances and soft tissues were well padded in the 
standard fashion.  Preoperative antibiotics were administered according to the 
appropriate timing schedule.  Care was taken to maintain appropriate perfusion 
pressures during anesthesia.  At the conclusion of the procedure, sponge and 
needle count were correct x 2.  



Final time out was undertaken by members of the operating team to confirm 
correct patient, correct levels and correct surgery.  An incision was then made 
over the intended surgical levels, and sharp dissection was carried out down to 
the posterior elements.  Soft tissues were elevated off the posterior elements 
in a subperiosteal manner, and a lateral radiograph was obtained to confirm 
correct level.  At this point, a rongeur was used to remove the spinous process 
of L4. The lamina was thinned in the midline, and a Luna curette was used to 
undermine the superior insertion of the ligamentum flavum on the inferior 
surface of the L4 lamina.  The canal was entered, and a Carlton elevator was 
utilized to separate dura from surrounding soft tissue and bone prior to use of 
the Kerrison punch.  A 4-0 Kerrison rongeur was then used to perform midline 
decompression.  At the superior aspect of this decompression, we encountered a 
large arachnoid cyst. We packed this of with a surgical david in hopes that it 
would not become a full thickness dural tear.  Unfortunately, during the 
lateral recess decompressions, the arachnoid cyst gave way, and a significant 
amount of spinal fluid began leaking.  We therefore packed that off again, and 
placed the patient in 5 degrees of Trendelenburg.  We proceeded with bilateral 
lateral recess decompressions, taking care to thoroughly decompress the lateral 
recesses at that L4-L5 level, and also ensure that the foramina for the L5 and 
the L4 nerves were well decompressed. Once this was accomplished, we turned our 
attention to placement of pedicle screws.  Appropriate starting points for 
pedicle screws were identified at approximately the junction of the pars 
interarticularis, the midpoint of the transverse process and the lateral aspect 
of the superior articular process.  A high-speed yoel was used to decorticate, 
and then a Lenke-type probe was used to advance resistance through the isthmus 
of the pedicle and into the vertebral body.  A ball tip feeler was then used to 
palpate the pedicle superiorly, inferiorly, medial and laterally as well as 
distally to ensure absence of bony breaching.  Once this was confirmed, 6.5 mm 
x 45 mm screws were placed bilaterally at L4 and bilaterally at L5.  All screws 
had good purchase, and neurophysiologic monitoring was used to test the screws, 
all of which tested well above expected levels.  Lateral radiograph was 
obtained to confirm correct placement of all screws.  



At this point, 2 L of sterile saline were used to irrigate the wound, and we 
then decorticated the transverse processes of L4 and L5 bilaterally.  Bone that 
had been previously removed during the laminectomy portion of the procedure was 
run through a bone mill and then packed in the lateral recesses.  Surgical 
patties were then removed from the durotomy, and two pieces of DuraGen were 
placed in a elizabeth cross fashion over the durotomy and the arachnoid cyst.  The 
entire laminectomy defect was then sealed utilizing DuraSeal.  Once this was 
completed, no CSF leakage was noted.  



The wound was then closed in layers using interrupted sutures for the deep 
fascia, interrupted sutures for the subcutaneous tissue and then a running 
subcuticular skin stitch.  Sponge and needle counts were correct x 2.



POSTOPERATIVE CARE PLAN

We will keep Mr. Griffin flat overnight to give his durotomy an opportunity to 
heal.  We will begin gradually sitting him up midmorning tomorrow.  He will 
likely discharge home on  or  of this week, and will follow up 
in my clinic in two weeks time for wound check and examination.

REASON FOR CONSULTATION:  Hemoperitoneum.

 

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS:  This is a 40-year-old female who underwent 
laparoscopic single-port supracervical hysterectomy today complicated by 
postoperative bleeding for which the patient was returned to the operating room 
for laparoscopy.  The patient subsequently remained intubated and was 
transferred to the intensive care unit.  She received 6 units of blood, 2 units 
of FFP and due to concerns for ongoing bleeding, the patient was returned to 
the operating room by Dr. Ruiz and I was asked to assist in her care.  



The patient was encountered on the operating room table and Dr. Ruiz 
performed midline laparotomy as dictated in his note.  At that time, a large 
amount of hemoperitoneum was encountered and I assisted in enlarging the 
laparotomy incisions superiorly packing off the abdomen and temporarily applied 
manual compression to her aorta due to hemodynamic instability.  There was 
subsequent return of adequate pressures and thorough exploration of the abdomen 
was next performed.  Lap pads were removed sequentially from 4 quadrants and 
upon inspection of the left upper quadrant, there was a large amount of blood 
and clot.  Due to concerns for a prior inadvertent splenic injury, the incision 
was further extended upwards toward the xiphoid and after evacuating blood and 
clot, examination of the spleen revealed this to be intact.  The anterior 
surface of the stomach was inspected and noted to be normal.  A nasogastric 
tube was advanced into the body of the stomach under direct palpation.  
Inspection of the right upper quadrant revealed no evidence of any liver 
injury.  Gallbladder appeared normal.  In the right lower quadrant, there was 
some blood within the right pericolic retroperitoneal tissues adjacent to the 
site where the patient had retroperitoneum opened during lysis of adhesions and 
apparent cauterization of endometriosis.  Careful inspection of this area did 
not reveal any active bleeding. The small bowel was run from the ligament of 
Treitz distally to the ileocecal valve and back again.  There was no evidence 
of injury to the small bowel or the small bowel mesentry.  Inspection of the 
retroperitoneum in the area of the aorta and the bifurcation revealed no 
hematoma or evidence of injury.  The large intestine was examined.  The cecum, 
appendix, ascending colon, transverse colon all appeared normal as did the 
descending colon, sigmoid, and rectum.  Within the omentum, there was clotted 
blood noted. There was some hematoma that was thought to be possibly due to 
small vessel bleeding within the omentum and this was ligated with 3-0 Vicryl.  
Remaining inspection revealed evidence of bleeding within the pelvis. This was 
dealt with as dictated in Dr. Ruiz's note.

 

IMPRESSION:  Hemoperitoneum secondary to postoperative bleeding, status post 
laparoscopic supracervical hysterectomy, as well as consumptive coagulopathy 
versus disseminated intravascular coagulation.

 

PLAN/RECOMMENDATIONS:  The patient will continue to be resuscitated and 
transfused per the rapid transfusion protocol in order to correct her anemia, 
thrombocytopenia, and coagulopathy.  Surgical associates will be available 
should additional surgical needs arise.

She was induced with multiple doses of cytotec and then pitocin. AROM was performed for clear fluid. She received epidural anesthesia .  tracing was reassuring with rare decels, + accels, and moderate variability. She progressed to complete/+1 and pushing commenced. Recurrent decels were noted with pushing but  recovered spontaneously after each contraction. After one hour, decision was made to stop pushing and allow to labor down in order for the mother to rest and to provide a period of time without pushing for  recovery. After approximately one hour, pushing was resumed. After approximately 1.5 hours of additional pushing, the station had descended to +2 station but would not descend further. Recurrent late and variable decelerations were noted and the patient reported exhaustion.  
We discussed a forceps assisted vaginal delivery versus continued pushing verus a  delivery. The risks and benefits were discussed of each. After consideration, the patient elected to proceed with a FAVD. Anesthesia was called and the patient was given an epidural redose.   �   position was determined to be LALO. The bladder was emptied with a catheter for 0 mL. The EFW was 3100 mL. Quinten-Morin forceps were opened and confirmed to articulate appropriately. The posterior and anterior blades were placed gently and without difficulty and articulated appropriately. The sagittal suture was palpated and confirmed to be equidistant from both blades, confirming appropriate placement. The patient pushed through the next three contractions with forceps assistance. A right mediolateral second degree episiotomy was cut. With her next contraction, the patient was again instructed to push with forceps assistance and the  head delivered in LALO. The forceps were disarticulated. A nuchal cord x1 was noted. The shoulders delivered spontaneously prior to reduction of the nuchal. The  was placed on the maternal abdomen and the nose and mouth were suctioned. The cords was clamped and cut after approximately 60 seconds of delay at the time of cessation of cord pulsations. The placenta delivered spontaneously with maternal pushing. Uterine atony was noted. The uterus was explored and no evidence of retained products of conception were found. Bleeding was managed with bimanual massage, IV infusion of pitocin, and cytotec 800mcg rectally. Uterine bleeding resolved.     Rectal exam confirmed that the mucosa was intact. The perineum was examined and the episiotomy was found to have extended to a third degree laceration with partial inclusion of the internal anal sphincter. The cervix and vagina were examined and a right sulcal laceration was noted. Ancef 2g was ordered and the perineum was cleansed with iodine. The  
internal anal sphincter was repaired in continuous fashion with 3-0 Vicryl. The ends of the external anal sphincter were grasped with Allis clamps and were repaired in end-to-end fashion with four interrupted sutures of 2-0 Vicryl. The remainder of the perineal laceration was then repaired in standard fashion using 2-0 Vicryl. The right sulcal laceration was then repaired with 3-0 Vicryl in continuous fashion. A superficial laceration was noted on the posterior vaginal mucosa, approximately 2cm in length proximal to the perineal laceration, and was repaired with a figure of eight. All lacerations were confirmed to be hemostatic. Bleeding was noted from the uterus and a small amount of clot was cleared from the lower uterine segment. Bleeding was monitored and was minimal.     Vaginal sweep was done, laps count was correct. The procedure and repair was discussed with the patient. Light grant from the forceps were noted on the 's bilateral cheeks, indicating appropriate placement. No bruising or lacerations on the  were noted.     The patient overall tolerated the procedure well. Mother and  were left to recovery in stable condition.      I returned to the room shortly after for complaints of patient lightheadedness and BP to 90/50s. Fluid bolus started. Vaginal bleeding was minimal. A vaginal sweep was performed and the uterus was confirmed to be firm with no clots. No vaginal masses were felt. Manual BP was 118/90. The patient reported improvement in her symptoms. A STAT CBC, coags, fibrinogen were ordered. Will continue to monitor.     Lizet Shipley
